content.title: About
content.content: Beef and potatoes, no sauce is a simple dish consisting of boiled or pan‑seared beef paired with boiled or roasted potatoes. It is popular worldwide as a hearty lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is one of the richest sources of iron and zinc.
Potatoes rank fourth among the most consumed foods globally after bread, rice and pasta.
In traditional Russian cuisine the dish is often served with mustard or sour cream, but without sauce it highlights the natural flavors.
When cooked properly, beef stays tender while potatoes become aromatic and slightly crisp on the outside.
The recipe can be easily adapted for dietary needs by swapping part of the beef for leaner meat.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in bioavailable iron
items.content: The iron in beef is readily absorbed, supporting healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Potassium and vitamin C in potatoes
items.content: Potatoes supply potassium for fluid balance and vitamin C to boost immunity.

items.title: Beta‑carotene in yellow potatoes
items.content: Provides provitamin A, beneficial for vision and skin health.

items.title: Moderate carbohydrate load when portioned
items.content: A balanced beef‑to‑potato ratio can fit into a moderate‑carb diet.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Fatty cuts of beef can raise cholesterol; choosing lean cuts is advisable.

items.title: Risk of overeating
items.content: The dish is calorie‑dense; portion control is important for weight‑management plans.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Acrylamide in over‑cooked potatoes
items.content: High‑temperature roasting can form acrylamide, a potential carcinogen.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, slicing the beef into strips and cutting the potatoes into wedges or cubes. Garnish with fresh herbs such as parsley or rosemary, and drizzle a little olive oil if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked beef and potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in separate portions.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate cereal flakes are dry grain flakes coated with a sweet chocolate glaze. They are intended for a quick breakfast, usually served with milk or yogurt. The flakes are crunchy, and the chocolate coating gives them a rich, sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial chocolate cereal appeared in the United States in the 1970s.
Chocolate flakes are often used in children's breakfasts and as a decorative topping for desserts.
The cocoa content of the glaze typically ranges from 10 % to 30 %, influencing flavor intensity.
Bright colors are often achieved with natural or artificial food colorings.
Some brands offer gluten‑free versions using rice or corn flakes.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates and a modest amount of fat provides a quick energy boost, ideal for starting the day.

items.title: Iron source
items.content: Fortified cereals are often enriched with iron, which is essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 present in fortified cereals support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: When eaten with milk, the cereal contributes additional calcium important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Chocolate antioxidants
items.content: The cocoa glaze contains flavonoids that may provide antioxidant benefits.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Chocolate cereals often contain a significant amount of added sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Ingredients may include milk, soy, nuts or gluten, requiring caution for people with allergies.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of sugar and fat, the cereal is relatively high in calories; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Some brands use partially hydrogenated oils that contain trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place a serving of flakes in a bowl, pour milk, yogurt, or a plant‑based beverage over them, and let sit for 1–2 minutes. The flakes can also be used in baking, desserts, smoothies, or as a crunchy topping for ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cereal in its original packaging or an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. When kept properly, it remains fresh for 6–12 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken cornbread is a savory baked loaf that combines tender chicken breast with a light, slightly sweet corn batter. It features a golden crust, moist crumb, and a subtle corn flavor, making it a satisfying main dish for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cornbread originates from Southern cuisine, where corn has long been a staple grain.
Adding chicken boosts the protein content without dramatically increasing fat.
Traditional recipes often include milk or buttermilk to create a fluffy texture.
Cornmeal is naturally gluten‑free, so the loaf can be made suitable for gluten‑intolerant diets.
The dish is commonly served with barbecue sauce or a honey‑mustard glaze.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The loaf contains niacin, vitamin B6, and folate, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Cornmeal adds fiber that aids healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Using lean chicken breast and minimal added oil keeps the saturated fat content modest.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Corn provides carotenoids and phenolic compounds that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken and should avoid the product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salty seasonings are added, the loaf can become high in sodium, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cornbread contains carbohydrates, so portion control is advisable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Undercooking risk
items.content: Insufficiently cooked chicken may harbor harmful bacteria; ensure the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chicken cornbread warm, sliced into wedges. It can be enjoyed on its own, used as a base for sandwiches, or paired with salads and dipping sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the loaf in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in the oven or microwave before serving.

chicken-drumstick-fried-coated-skin-coat.title: Chicken drumstick, fried, coated, skin/coating edible, from raw

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken drumsticks are the lower leg portion of the bird, containing meat, skin and a small amount of bone. When deep‑fried in a coating, they develop a crunchy crust while the interior stays juicy. The product is made from raw meat (code 817) and is commonly served hot as a snack or main dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks are a staple of street food and fast‑food menus because of their convenient size and flavor.
The coating can be made from wheat flour, breadcrumbs, spices and sometimes corn starch, giving extra crunch.
Deep‑frying at 175‑190 °C creates a golden crust and locks moisture inside the meat.
Chicken is one of the most affordable sources of protein worldwide.
Edible skin contains collagen, which turns partially into gelatin during cooking.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken drumsticks provide high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken delivers iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: When prepared without sugary sauces, drumsticks fit well into low‑carb diets.

items.title: Collagen from skin
items.content: Edible skin contains collagen, which may benefit skin and joint health.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds saturated and trans fats, so consumption should be moderate.

items.title: Salt and seasonings
items.content: Coatings often contain salt and flavor enhancers, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Contamination if undercooked
items.content: Insufficient frying temperature can leave harmful bacteria (Salmonella, Campylobacter) alive.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A typical serving (≈100 g) of fried coated drumstick provides about 250–300 kcal.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the drumsticks hot, often with dipping sauces such as barbecue, mayo or spicy sauce. Eat with your hands, pulling the meat off the bone. The skin and coating are eaten together with the meat. For a lighter option, bake in the oven without added oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked drumsticks refrigerated at +4 °C for up to 2‑3 days in an airtight container. For longer storage, freeze at -18 °C, where they retain quality for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Iced tea with lemonade is a refreshing non‑alcoholic beverage that blends flavorful tea with a sweet hint of lemonade. It is usually made from black or green tea, sweetened with sugar or syrup, and combined with lemon juice, sometimes topped with sparkling water.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink is especially popular in summer and is often served over ice with a lemon wedge.
The tea‑lemonade combination originated in the United States in the early 20th century as an alternative to carbonated sodas.
Tea provides a mild dose of caffeine, while lemon juice adds vitamin C.
Variations may include mint, ginger, berries, or flavored syrups such as peach or strawberry.
Because it is easy to make at home, many people prepare it using bagged tea and ready‑made lemonade concentrate.

items.title: Antioxidants from tea
items.content: Black and green tea are rich in polyphenols, which help combat free radicals and support heart health.

items.title: Vitamin C from lemon
items.content: Lemon juice is a good source of vitamin C, which contributes to immune system function.

items.title: Mild hydration
items.content: The beverage provides water and electrolytes, aiding hydration especially in hot weather.

items.title: Gentle energy boost
items.content: Caffeine from tea offers a subtle energy lift without sharp blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Lemon juice can stimulate gastric secretions, helping with digestion.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Commercial versions often contain high amounts of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of tooth decay.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Tea’s caffeine may cause insomnia or jitteriness in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Lemon juice raises the drink’s acidity, which may irritate the stomach of people with gastritis or reflux.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to citrus fruits, which can trigger skin reactions or swelling.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the iced tea lemonade chilled, over ice, with a lemon slice. You can add fresh mint, berries, or a splash of ginger syrup for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared drink in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. Over longer storage the flavor may change and sugar can crystallize.

content.title: About
content.content: Mango nectar is a sweet beverage made from the pulp of ripe mangoes, sugar and water. It has a bright tropical aroma, a rich mango flavor and a light texture. It is often enjoyed as a refreshing drink, a cocktail ingredient, or a dessert topping.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mango is known as the “king of fruits” in India and Southeast Asia.
Nectar retains most of the vitamin C and carotenoids found in fresh mango.
Traditionally, mango nectar was prepared by slowly simmering the pulp with sugar to intensify the aroma.
In some countries the nectar is served hot during winter as a warming drink.
There are many mango varieties, each giving the nectar a distinct taste and color.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A, important for vision and skin health.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in fluid balance and helps maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: The nectar contains a modest amount of soluble fiber that can support digestion.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Sugars in the nectar quickly replenish energy, making it a good post‑exercise drink.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Added sugar can raise blood glucose levels and contribute to weight gain if consumed in excess.

items.title: Mango allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mango proteins, resulting in skin rashes or swelling.

items.title: Presence of preservatives
items.content: Commercial versions often contain preservatives and flavor enhancers that may be undesirable for sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mango nectar can be enjoyed chilled on its own, used in smoothies, cocktails, ice cream, desserts, or as a sweetener for sauces and marinades.

content.title: Storage
content.content: After opening, keep the nectar refrigerated in a sealed bottle and consume within 5‑7 days. Unopened containers should be stored in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight.

content.title: About
content.content: Raw plantain is an unripe fruit of the banana plant (Musa spp.) that has a firmer texture and less sweetness than ripe bananas. The fruits are typically green, slightly starchy, and are commonly used as a vegetable in cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Raw plantain is often called “green banana” and is a staple in African, Caribbean, and South Asian cuisines.
Compared with ripe bananas, raw plantain contains more resistant starch, which acts as a prebiotic.
The fruits grow in bunches of 10–20 and can reach up to 30 cm in length.
Raw plantain is frequently fried, boiled, or baked, and in some cultures it is milled into flour.
Its starchy texture makes it a good potato substitute in gluten‑free recipes.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Raw plantain provides a good amount of vitamin C, supporting immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes digestive health and can aid in blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Resistant starch
items.content: Resistant starch acts as a prebiotic, fostering beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Raw plantain is virtually fat‑free, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Solanine content
items.content: Improperly stored or damaged raw plantain may develop solanine, a toxin that can cause gastrointestinal upset.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to banana family plants, experiencing skin rashes or swelling.

items.title: Excess potassium
items.content: People with kidney disease should limit raw plantain intake due to its high potassium levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw plantain is usually peeled and prepared by frying, boiling in stews, baking, or mashing. It can be sliced thinly for chips or used as a potato alternative in casseroles. Boiling the pieces for 5–10 minutes before cooking helps reduce bitterness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw plantain in a cool, dry place, preferably in the refrigerator. At room temperature the fruit darkens quickly and loses texture. In the fridge it keeps for up to 5 days; for longer storage, peel, slice, and freeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork and beans is a canned dish made of cooked white beans, pieces of pork, tomato sauce and seasonings. It is popular in the United States and many other countries as a quick, hearty meal or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial pork and beans recipe appeared in the US in the late 19th century.
Traditionally it was cooked in iron kettles over an open fire and then canned in glass jars.
Original recipes used pork shoulder, but today leaner cuts are often used.
The beans are usually pre‑soaked and boiled until tender, preserving their nutrients.
In the US pork and beans are often served with bread, rice or mashed potatoes.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The combination of beans and pork provides a high‑quality complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Beans supply soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product contains thiamine, niacin and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides iron, magnesium, phosphorus and potassium, vital for blood formation, nerve function and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Low glycemic carbohydrates
items.content: Beans contain complex carbs that raise blood glucose slowly, helping to control appetite.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned versions often contain a lot of salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Fat content from pork
items.content: Some recipes use fatty pork cuts, increasing calories and saturated fat.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A minority of individuals may be allergic to beans.

items.title: Bacterial contamination if stored improperly
items.content: Damaged or opened cans left at room temperature for long periods can become a source of pathogens.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat pork and beans in the microwave or on the stove, serve as a standalone dish, add to chili, casseroles, or use as a filling for tortillas.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened can in a cool, dry place. After opening, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator and consume within 3‑4 days.
